what_its_for: Infliximab-axxq is used to treat several conditions where your immune system attacks your own body. These include rheumatoid arthritis (joint pain and swelling), Crohn's disease (inflammation of the digestive tract), ulcerative colitis (inflammation of the large intestine), ankylosing spondylitis (spine inflammation), psoriatic arthritis (joint inflammation with psoriasis), and plaque psoriasis (red, scaly skin patches). It works by blocking a protein in your body called TNF-alpha that causes inflammation.
how_to_take: Infliximab-axxq is NOT a pill or injection you give yourself at home. It is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion, meaning it is dripped slowly into a vein through a needle. A nurse or doctor will give you this medicine in a clinic, hospital, or infusion center. Each infusion usually takes about 2 hours. You will be watched closely during and after your infusion for any reactions. Do not try to give this medicine to yourself at home.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your weight and the condition being treated. The dose is usually given in milligrams per kilogram of body weight. For most conditions, you will receive infusions at Week 0, Week 2, and Week 6, and then every 6 to 8 weeks after that for maintenance. Your doctor may adjust your dose or schedule depending on how well the medicine is working for you. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions.
missed_dose: Because this medicine is given by a healthcare provider, missing a dose is not something you manage on your own. If you need to reschedule or miss your infusion appointment, call your doctor's office or infusion center as soon as possible. Do not try to double up on doses. Your doctor will let you know when to come in for your next infusion.
storage: You do not need to store this medicine at home since it is prepared and given by healthcare professionals. The prepared infusion solution should be used within 3 hours of preparation if kept at room temperature, or within 24 hours if kept in the refrigerator. The original vials must be kept refrigerated between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Keep it away from freezing and direct light. Do not use the medicine if it looks cloudy, has visible particles, or has changed color.
what_to_avoid: Avoid contact with people who are sick or have infections, as this medicine weakens your immune system and makes it harder for your body to fight germs. Do not receive any live vaccines (such as the chickenpox vaccine, measles-mumps-rubella, or live flu nasal spray) while using this medicine without talking to your doctor first. Avoid excessive sun exposure and use sunscreen since this medicine may increase your risk of skin cancer. Tell your doctor if you drink alcohol regularly. Avoid starting any new prescription or over-the-counter medications, vitamins, or supplements without checking with your doctor first.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or get emergency help if you experience: chest pain, shortness of breath, or difficulty breathing; signs of a serious infection such as fever, chills, cough, painful urination, or wounds that won't heal; signs of an allergic reaction such as hives, itching, rash, swollen face, lips, tongue, or throat; numbness or tingling in your hands or feet; vision changes; unusual bruising or bleeding; symptoms of liver problems such as yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, or severe stomach pain; or new or worsening heart failure symptoms like swelling in your legs or ankles. Also tell your doctor if you notice any new lumps or bumps, unexplained weight loss, or night sweats, as this medicine may increase the risk of certain cancers.
when_it_works: You may start to feel some improvement within 2 to 6 weeks after starting treatment, but it can take up to 3 months or longer to feel the full benefit. Some people notice reduced pain, swelling, and stiffness fairly quickly, while others may take more time. It is important to keep all your scheduled infusion appointments even if you do not feel better right away. Do not stop treatment without talking to your doctor first.
special_populations: Older adults (65 years and older) may have a higher risk of serious infections while taking this medicine and should be monitored more closely. This medicine is approved for use in children (6 years and older) for Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis. If you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant, talk to your doctor before using this medicine, as it may affect the baby. Babies born to mothers who used this medicine during pregnancy should not receive live vaccines for at least 6 months after birth. If you are breastfeeding, talk to your doctor since it is not fully known whether this medicine passes into breast milk. People with a history of tuberculosis (TB), hepatitis B, heart failure, multiple sclerosis, or certain cancers should discuss the risks carefully with their doctor before starting this medicine.
